sections.title: Reading Comprehension · Passage C
sections.intro: Read the adapted article about coyotes and answer questions 15–24. A photograph description and vocabulary notes are included with the transcript.

passage.title: Coyotes Have Expanded Their Range to 49 States—And Show No Signs of Stopping
passage.credit: —Christine Dell’Amore · excerpted and adapted from “Coyotes Have Expanded Their Range to 49 States—And Show No Signs of Stopping” · www.nationalgeographic.com, November 29, 2019

lines.text: Photograph: A coyote walks through a wooded area.
CHICAGO—She pops up suddenly from behind a green tarp and trots through the
construction site, pausing every so often to swivel her large, triangular ears. The *beep beep*
*beep* of a cement paver and the deafening roar of buzzsaws are just background noise
A few weeks ago her mate for life, 1244, was shot near this new high school going up
outside Chicago. Now Lauren Ross, a field technician with the Max McGraw Wildlife
Foundation, has pinpointed the radio-collared female’s location with a telemetry unit, the
constant ping revealing her exact location. Even so, it’s rare to see urban coyotes during the
day, as most have learned to be active at night to avoid people. But 1242 has pups to feed.
And in the indefatigable¹ coyote spirit—that same quality that has propelled the predator
into every corner of the United States—this lanky single mother is making it work without
her partner.
“We consistently underestimate this animal and its ability to adjust and adapt,” says
Stan Gehrt, a wildlife ecologist with Ohio State University and the Max McGraw Wildlife
Foundation. Gehrt has studied Chicago’s coyotes since 2000, not long after the animals
surfaced in the nation’s third biggest city. “They push the boundaries of what we perceive to
be constraints,” Gehrt says.
For instance, at the beginning of his research, he thought coyotes would be restricted
to parks and green spaces. He was wrong. “Now we have coyotes everywhere—every
neighborhood, every suburban city, and downtown. The only place we don’t have them is
airports, and that’s because they kill them.”
Native to the western two-thirds of the United States, coyotes began dramatically
expanding their range in the early 1900s. They’ve increased their habitat across North
America by 40 percent since the 1950s—twice the rate of any other North American
carnivore—and now live in every U.S. state but Hawaii. The near-extinction of wolves, the
crash of the coyote pelt market, and the explosion of food-rich suburbs fueled their rise, as
did their innate tenacity forged by a million years of evolution.
“They have this amazing balance between being bold enough to hunt, attack, and kill
something and being shy or savvy enough to avoid being killed themselves,” Gehrt says. And
they’ve achieved this dramatic increase despite being one of the most persecuted animals in
the U.S. At least 400,000 coyotes are exterminated each year, with the federal government
killing around 80,000.
From New York City (one daring individual hopped onto a roof in Queens) to the Florida
Keys to the Hollywood Hills, no city or climate seems off limits. Coyotes recently migrated
as far south as Panama, where they’re now poised to enter South America for the first time.
When will they stop? That’s the question that fascinates many urban ecologists. So far
coyotes seem to have weathered most traditional population checks, such as disease.
“What’s striking is almost all eastern states show exponential growth,” says Roland Kays,
a zoologist at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and North Carolina State
University in Raleigh, who studies how coyotes evolved and spread across the continent.
“There’s no leveling off in most places.”
That’s why Gehrt’s Urban Coyote Research Project in Chicago—and many similar
initiatives² in New York, Vancouver, Los Angeles, Denver, Washington D.C., San Francisco,
and elsewhere—are busy trying to figure out how people can best coexist with a predator
that’s here to stay. …
Though much is made of coyotes’ flexibility, they’re rigid in two regards: their
monogamy—generally both parents raise a litter of pups together—and in their need for a
defined territory. This territorialism, says Gehrt, could be a factor that will limit their spread.
Common sense says that when coyotes run out of room, their population should drop.
But that’s not what’s happening in Chicago. Instead, the animals are carving out niches in the
most impractical and dangerous of places, such as busy downtown streets. If a young coyote
simply can’t find a home, its parents will sometimes cede³ part of their territory, a process
called “budding.”
The territorial instinct is also why killing coyotes with the goal of reducing their numbers—
called lethal control—doesn’t usually work. Like the game Whac-a-Mole, killing coyotes only
creates a habitat vacuum, giving their competitors a chance to move in. Beyond that, coyote
biology is primed for persecution: When the rate of killing goes up, young coyotes mature
faster, and females produce larger litters.
Disease is another factor that usually limits wildlife populations, Gehrt notes. Canine
distemper, for example, often breaks out among wild coyotes. But except for a few cases of
mange and getting hit by cars—their primary cause of death—Chicago’s coyotes are oddly
healthy, living even longer than rural coyotes.
According to analyses of coyote trapping records in the eastern U.S. by Roland Kays,
the North Carolina zoologist, it’s possible that coyote populations have reached their limit—
called the carrying capacity—in Maine and New Hampshire, the first eastern states they
colonized. But it’s still too early to say for sure, Kays cautions.
Stewart Breck, a research wildlife biologist with the U.S. Department of Agriculture in
Denver, says that the coyote population in that city has remained stable over the past decade,
indicating that it has reached carrying capacity.
But, he says, “As they continue to expand their distribution on a geographic level
[throughout the Americas], what are the limits?”
For some animals with specialized diets, food availability can also restrict population
growth. But coyotes are omnivores, often eating fruit and vegetables—both of which are in
plentiful supply in the suburbs. Yet most urban coyotes still eat a lot of wild prey—particularly
rabbits and squirrels—instead of trash or human food.
Because many coyotes dwell in areas that blur the line between wild and urban, figuring
out how to predict their patterns is complex. Busse Woods, [in Chicago] for example, may
look natural, but it’s an illusion, Gehrt says. At least 2.5 million people come here every year,
and the park is hemmed in by neighborhoods and busy roads.
“Even in what you consider the most protected, natural areas, those coyotes are being
born and raised around people and dogs.”
So far, reported run-ins with people haven’t increased, even as Chicago’s coyote
population continues to grow—there are now up to 4,000 in Cook County alone. But, Gehrt
says, “The question is, year after year, generation after generation, will they continue to have
that healthy fear of people?” …
Like them or not, coyotes are thriving in our human-dominated era—the Anthropocene—
when most species aren’t, Kays notes. “It’s a really interesting evolution story that’s happening
right under our noses.” …
¹ indefatigable — unrelenting
² initiatives — programs
³ cede — transfer or surrender

questions.prompt: A purpose of the anecdote in the first paragraph is to

choices.text: introduce opposing views
arouse reader curiosity
establish a prediction
intensify a bias

questions.explanation: The opening shows a coyote moving through a noisy construction site and identifies her only as “1242.” This vivid, unusual scene invites readers to wonder about the animal before the article explains the research.

questions.prompt: The information presented about coyotes 1244 and 1242 (lines 5 through 9) implies that scientists have been

choices.text: trying to relocate the pair
trying to domesticate the pair
tracking the pair for study
tracking the pair for elimination

questions.explanation: The female wears a radio collar, and a field technician locates her with a telemetry unit. Those details show the coyotes are being monitored for research, not domesticated or targeted for removal.

questions.prompt: The description of the coyote in lines 10 through 12 exhibits a tone of

choices.text: fear of the coyote’s increasing aggressiveness
respect for the coyote’s resourcefulness
sentimentality toward the coyote’s offspring
concern over the coyote’s declining population

questions.explanation: Calling 1242 an “indefatigable” single mother who is “making it work” without her mate emphasizes her persistence and adaptability. The wording conveys respect for her resourcefulness.

questions.prompt: The primary function of lines 13 through 21 is to

choices.text: analyze the methodology of previous coyote studies
clarify the rationale for coyote eradication efforts
justify the resources needed to preserve coyote populations
refute the previous assumptions made about coyote habitats

questions.explanation: Gehrt first expected coyotes to remain in parks and green spaces, but he now finds them in neighborhoods and downtown too. The evidence corrects his earlier assumption about where they can live.

questions.prompt: According to lines 22 through 27, the reader can infer that the coyote population has expanded predominately as a result of

choices.text: trends in the human community
patterns in the activities of other predators
learning to avoid recreational hunters
choosing to abandon previous habitats

questions.explanation: The passage attributes expansion to wolf near-extinction, the collapse of the pelt market, and food-rich suburbs. These human-driven environmental and economic changes largely explain why coyotes spread.

questions.prompt: The phrase “innate tenacity” (line 27) refers to the coyotes’

choices.text: interdependence with rival species
merging with domesticated populations
adaptability to changing circumstances
migration to unprotected areas

questions.explanation: “Innate” means inborn and “tenacity” means persistence. In context, coyotes survive and spread despite changed habitats and pressures, showing a built-in ability to adjust to circumstances.

questions.prompt: The information in lines 28 through 32 presents

choices.text: a foreshadowing of the coyotes’ fate
a point of view that coyote numbers must be protected
an allusion to previous coyote population studies
an irony in the coyotes’ surging numbers

questions.explanation: Coyotes have expanded dramatically even though hundreds of thousands are killed each year. Their growing numbers despite heavy persecution form the irony emphasized in these lines.

questions.prompt: Lines 33 through 35 contribute to a central idea that coyotes

choices.text: have the ability to avoid public places
have the ability to respond to circumstances
tend to resist seasonal changes
tend to prefer stable conditions

questions.explanation: The article lists coyotes living from New York City to the Florida Keys and Hollywood Hills, and even moving toward South America. Success across such different places shows their responsiveness to new conditions.

questions.prompt: An effect of the “budding” process (line 53) is that

choices.text: larger numbers of coyotes are occupying less space
larger hunting territories are attracting more coyotes
fewer successful families are led by adult coyotes
fewer mated coyotes are reproducing in less space

questions.explanation: When a young coyote cannot find territory, its parents may give up part of theirs. Dividing existing territory lets more coyotes occupy the same general area in smaller individual spaces.

questions.prompt: Lines 76 through 85 contribute to a central idea by suggesting that

choices.text: the identification of habitats for coyotes will be achieved through regulation
coyotes will continue to seek areas with smaller human populations
the interaction between humans and coyotes is inevitable
coyotes will expand to dominate park wildlife

questions.explanation: The article says even seemingly natural areas are surrounded by people and roads, coyotes grow up near people and dogs, and Chicago’s coyote population is growing. Human–coyote encounters are therefore difficult to avoid.
